contributions.statement: Before writing agent-facing documentation in bulk for the ingestion repos, measure it with a paired ablation on the team's own codebase questions (same agent and same system prompt, doc comments, comments and doc files stripped vs present, scored per question), split by whether the answer lives in code or only in docs, because here docs added +0.05 to +0.09 (0-1 judged score, 100 questions) on doc-sourced questions and about 0 on code-answerable ones.
contributions.evidence: §5.1 Table 3 (closed-book / code-only / documented arms). Table 5 (doc-dependent Δdoc +0.053 to +0.091, all four models). Table 6 (code-derivable mean Δdoc +0.006; Claude +0.026, Gemini -0.018). App. H paired bootstrap over tasks. Caveats: doc-dependent gold answers were written from the docs (§4.5), so the documented arm is favoured by construction; the documented arm also got a 'search docs first' prompt (§6.1); one unvalidated GPT-5.4 judge; one run per cell; Python-only AST stripping.
relative_to: 2607.27250 AGENTS.md present/absent ablation on patch tasks found no correctness effect
2609.22259 documented semantic content is what moves accuracy

contributions.statement: Spend documentation written for agents or new developers on design rationale, deprecations and edge-case caveats that the code cannot show, not on restating what the code does, because a code-reading agent already scored about 0.86 on doc-sourced questions without the docs, and adding them mainly raised completeness (+0.53 to +0.75 on a 0-5 axis) while adding about 0 on code-answerable questions.
contributions.evidence: Table 5 (code-only mean 0.860 vs documented 0.931 on doc-dependent tasks). Table 7 (completeness gains +0.53 to +0.75, accuracy +0.31 to +0.47, specificity saturated at >=4.78). Table 6 (code-derivable Δdoc about 0). Caveats: famous Python libraries with closed-book already 0.63 on these questions, so private domain code will lean on docs more; gold answers written from the docs; doc-first prompt confound; the search tool did not cover .md/.rst files (§4.3).
relative_to: known practice: comments should explain why, not what
2607.27250 write AGENTS.md as operational warnings rather than general repository knowledge

contributions.statement: Build an onboarding quiz or codebase-QA eval set from the team's repos answer-first (an agent writes the answer with at least three file-and-function evidence items whose paths are checked against the filesystem, then the question and a key-point rubric are derived from it) and have a human confirm every answer, because this pipeline's LLM-only fact-check passed just 38.4% outright and kept the 61.6% marked 'warn'.
contributions.evidence: §4.3 (agentic answer generation, >=3 code evidence items, key-file paths validated with re-prompt). §4.6 (question and rubric derived from the verified answer). §8 Limitations (38.4% pass / 61.6% warn, no human validation). Caveats: answer-first is never compared with question-first, so its claimed reduction of ill-posed questions is unmeasured.
relative_to: SWE-QA-Pro gold answers written by an agent and validated by humans (paper ref [3])
2605.08366 do not publish agent onboarding answers without expert review

contributions.statement: Give a codebase-QA agent read access to the repositories with even a plain toolset (regex search, directory listing, file reads) rather than asking a model with no repository access. In this study four models gained +0.23 on doc-sourced and +0.36 on code-sourced questions (0-1 judged score).
contributions.evidence: Tables 5-6 and App. H (all code-only minus closed-book deltas p<0.001; robust to dropping the specificity axis, recomputed from Table 7). Caveats: closed-book is the only comparator; famous repositories; one judge; one run per cell.
relative_to: 2608.24221 exploration agent beats one-shot embedding RAG on repository QA, including a Java subset
known practice: repository-grounded retrieval beats closed-book answers on repository-specific questions

reason: What survives is a measurement method, not a finding. The paired stripped-vs-documented ablation, split by where the answer lives, is a cheap way for the team to test whether its domain docs help an agent, and it points docs at rationale and caveats. Its numbers are weak: doc-sourced gold answers were written from the docs, the documented arm got a doc-first prompt, and one unvalidated judge scored everything. The only moderate result, that code access beats closed-book, restates 2608.24221 and known practice.
